Uzbekistan Faces Widespread Disruption as General Strike Halts Key Sectors

A nationwide general strike that began early Monday has brought significant disruption to economic activity across Uzbekistan, with workers from the transport, manufacturing, and public sectors walking out in a coordinated protest. The strike, organized by the Uzbek Federation of Trade Unions (UFTU), is the largest the country has seen in over a decade and is ongoing at the time of writing.

Public transport in Tashkent and other major cities has been severely affected, with metro and bus services operating at reduced capacity. The Ministry of Transport reported that only 30% of scheduled buses were running in the capital by midday. Airports in Samarkand and Fergana experienced delays as ground staff joined the stoppage, though air traffic controllers continued to work.

Manufacturing centres in the Navoi and Jizzakh regions have also scaled back operations. The Uzbek Industrial Association stated that output in local factories dropped by up to 60% on Monday and Tuesday. “The impact is already visible in the logistics chain, with shipments of goods significantly delayed,” said Timur Kadirov, head of market analysis at Asia Insight Advisors, a local consultancy.

The strike was called in response to ongoing disputes over wage levels and working conditions. UFTU Chairwoman Dilshoda Rasulova said in a statement, “Our members have waited too long for meaningful improvements. We are ready to negotiate, but our demands must be addressed.” The government has urged a swift return to work and pledged to open talks, with Deputy Prime Minister Alisher Ergashev telling reporters, “We recognize the concerns of workers, but we must restore normal operations to protect Uzbekistan’s economy.”

Retail and food supply chains have also been disrupted, especially in regional centres where fewer trucks are making deliveries. The Uzbekistan Retailers’ Council estimated that store inventories in Andijan and Namangan could fall by up to 40% if the strike continues for another week.

Economic analysts warn that a protracted strike could erode recent gains in foreign investment and GDP growth. “The longer this lasts, the higher the risk of lasting economic damage,” said Daler Bakhromov, senior economist at Silk Road Economic Review. Negotiations between union leaders and government officials are expected to resume later this week.
